title: Human–Wildlife Conflicts Around Taï National Park (Côte D'ivoire)
content:
ABSTRACT

Human–wildlife conflicts (HWC) threaten both rural livelihoods and wildlife conservation. Around Taï National Park, one of the last large, protected rainforests in West Africa, these conflicts are poorly documented. Here we described the types of conflict, identified the species involved and assessed their perceived impacts. In July 2022, we interviewed 489 household heads in 22 localities across the park's five management sectors, as well as 31 key informants from local institutions. Overall, 83.0% of households reported at least one type of damage. Crop raiding was the most common (82.4%), followed by losses of stored harvests (50.7%), attacks on domestic animals (38.7%) and attacks or threats to people (8.6%). The species reported differed strongly among sectors (p < 0.001). In the south (Djapadji, Djouroutou), large mammals dominated: Syncerus caffer nanus, Loxodonta cyclotis and primates. In the north and east (Soubré, ADK/V6), rodents, duikers and predators of small livestock dominated. Fear for one's life was mainly associated with having been attacked (adjusted odds ratio, aOR = 13.1) and with reporting megafauna (aOR = 3.1). Only 8.6% of households reported damage to the authorities, mostly because they did not know whom to contact or feared sanctions. Nine of 11 administrative authorities were unaware of any case. Protection methods were basic, and 9.7% of households used lethal or harmful methods such as snares, poison or fire. HWCs management should therefore be adapted to each sector and supported by an accessible reporting system.
